blocks.prompt: The Plant With No Wood
blocks.text: A banana plant is not a tree. A tree has hard wood inside it. A banana plant has no wood at all. Its tall trunk is made of leaves, rolled up tight like a roll of paper towels. That is why a big wind can knock a banana plant flat. The plant grows fast. In about nine months it is taller than your front door. Then it makes one huge bunch of bananas. The bunch can hold a hundred of them. After that, the whole plant dies. But a little baby plant is already growing beside it. The baby takes over. It makes the next bunch.

blocks.prompt: Bananas Grow Up, Not Down
blocks.text: When a banana plant is ready, a huge purple bud pushes out of the top and bends over toward the ground. Small bananas form along the hanging stalk in neat rows. Each row is called a hand, and each banana in the row is called a finger. Here is the strange part. The bananas start out pointing down, because that is the way the stalk hangs. Then they turn around. Growing plants reach toward light, and the light is above them, so every little banana curves upward as it grows. That gentle curve in your lunch box is a banana bending toward the sun. Bananas are picked while they are still green and hard. Inside a green banana, the sweetness is locked away as starch, the same stuff that fills a potato. As the banana ripens, it slowly turns that starch into sugar. The green fades and the yellow underneath shows through. A banana ripens itself using a gas called ethylene, and it shares that gas with any fruit sitting nearby. Put one banana in a bowl of apples and the whole bowl ripens faster.

blocks.prompt: Every Banana Is the Same Banana
blocks.text: Pick up a banana in a store in Ohio, then pick one up in a store in Norway. There is a good chance those two bananas are not just the same kind of fruit. They are the same plant. Almost every banana sold around the world is a variety called the Cavendish, and Cavendish plants are not grown from seeds. They are grown from suckers, the baby shoots that push up at the base of an older plant. Cut one off, plant it, and it becomes an exact copy of its parent. Do that for decades, across farms in a dozen countries, and you get billions of bananas that are all, genetically, one banana. Look closely inside the next one you eat. You will see a line of tiny black specks down the middle. Those are seeds that never finished forming. A wild banana is nothing like this. It is short and stubby and packed with hard black seeds the size of peppercorns, and you would spit out more than you swallowed. The soft, seedless banana in your hand is not something nature made on its own. Farmers in New Guinea began shaping it thousands of years ago by keeping and replanting the rare plants that made sweet fruit with almost no seed. Being a copy has a cost. Sameness means that whatever can kill one banana plant can kill all of them. That has already happened once. Until the 1950s the world ate a different variety called the Gros Michel. A fungus that lives in soil, known as Panama disease, found it, spread from farm to farm, and wiped it out of the export trade. Growers replaced it with the Cavendish, which that fungus could not touch. For about sixty years, that looked like the end of the story.

blocks.prompt: The Green Fruit That Crosses an Ocean
blocks.text: The banana in your kitchen is one of the most carefully engineered objects in your house, and almost none of that engineering shows. Start on the farm. A banana bunch is cut down while every finger is still hard and dark green, weeks before anyone would want to eat it. This is deliberate. A ripe banana is a soft bag of sugar that bruises if you look at it too long, and it would not survive a ship. A green one will. The bunch is washed, cut into hands, boxed, and loaded into a refrigerated vessel held at about 13 degrees Celsius, which is roughly 56 degrees Fahrenheit. That temperature is chosen with real care. Any warmer and the fruit ripens at sea and arrives as mush. Any colder and the banana suffers what the trade calls chilling injury, turning a dull gray and refusing to ripen at all, ever. Weeks later the boxes reach a port and go into sealed ripening rooms. There the fruit is dosed with ethylene, the same gas a banana produces naturally when it decides its own time has come. The gas flips a switch. Enzymes inside the fruit begin snapping long starch chains into sugars, the green chlorophyll drains away and lets the yellow underneath show, and the flesh softens. Ripening crews can dial the whole process to a schedule, so a store receives fruit that turns yellow on the shelf rather than in the truck. All of that precision rests on a single plant. The Cavendish is a clone, propagated from cuttings rather than seed, which means the entire global trade is one genetic individual grown a few billion times over. The industry already knows what that costs. It lost its previous variety, the Gros Michel, to a soil fungus in the middle of the twentieth century, and it survived only because the Cavendish happened to resist that particular strain. The fungus came back. A newer strain called Tropical Race 4 appeared in Asia around 1990, and the Cavendish has no defense against it. It lives in soil, it can ride to a clean farm on a boot or a truck tire, and it can wait in the ground for decades. Since then it has reached Australia, Africa, the Middle East, and, in 2019, Colombia. No spray cures it. The real answers are the slow ones: new varieties bred or gene-edited to resist it, and farms that stop betting everything on one plant.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Musa acuminata: botanically a berry, not a tree fruit
The pseudostem is packed leaf sheaths, no wood
Cavendish is seedless and propagated only by cuttings
Gros Michel fell to Panama disease in the 1950s
Tropical Race 4 blocks the plant's water vessels
TR4 can lie dormant in soil for thirty years
Domesticated in New Guinea about 7,000 years ago

blocks.prompt: Forever Yellow: The Fruit With No Plan B
blocks.text: There is a strong chance that every banana you have ever eaten came from the same plant. Not the same kind of plant. The same plant. The banana of global trade is a variety called the Cavendish, and it does not reproduce the way a fruit is supposed to. It has no working seeds. Those tiny black flecks running down the center of the flesh are ovules that never developed, leftovers of a sexual system the plant no longer uses. Cavendish bananas are propagated instead from suckers, shoots that push up from the base of a mature plant and can be cut away and replanted. Every one of those shoots is a genetic copy of its parent. Repeat that operation for decades, across plantations in Ecuador, Costa Rica, the Philippines and a dozen other countries, and the result is not really a population. It is a single genetic individual, grown a few billion times over. None of this is an accident of nature. Wild bananas are squat, seed-packed things, closer to gravel than to fruit. The banana you know is the product of thousands of years of human selection that began in New Guinea, where farmers kept replanting the rare mutant plants that produced sweet flesh and almost no seed. That choice was a trade. Seedlessness bought us an edible fruit and cost the plant its ability to shuffle its own genes. Every improvement since has had to be made by people, because the plant can no longer make one on its own. Uniformity is also, commercially, the product. A supermarket wants fruit that ripens on a predictable schedule, survives a two-week ocean crossing at 13 degrees Celsius, and looks identical in every store in every country. A clone delivers exactly that. The banana became cheap, abundant and reliable precisely because it stopped varying. The bill for that arrangement has come due once already. Until the 1950s the export banana was a different variety, the Gros Michel. A soil-borne fungus called Fusarium wilt, known in the trade as Panama disease, moved through the plantations of Central America and destroyed them. There was no cure, because there is no practical way to sterilize soil across thousands of acres. The industry survived by switching wholesale to the Cavendish, which happened to be immune to that particular strain. It was not a solution. It was a substitution, and it bought roughly sixty years. Around 1990 a new strain surfaced in Taiwan. Researchers call it Tropical Race 4, and the Cavendish has no resistance to it. The fungus plugs the plant's water vessels from the inside, so the leaves yellow, the crown collapses, and the plant starves standing up. TR4 lives in soil, travels on a boot sole or a truck tire or a bag of dirt, and can lie dormant in a field for thirty years. Nothing sprays it away. It has since been confirmed in Australia, China, the Middle East, Mozambique and, in 2019, Colombia, which placed it inside the hemisphere that grows most of the fruit sold in the United States. This is the same mistake, made twice. The response, at least, is more interesting than last time. Researchers are breeding and gene-editing resistant lines. Seed banks are preserving hundreds of banana varieties most of us have never tasted. Some growers are quietly planting mixed fields instead of endless identical rows. Whether the Cavendish itself survives matters less than the lesson underneath it. A crop that cannot change is a crop that is waiting.
